# Agentmux

iOS, iPadOS and Android client for SSH, persistent tmux sessions, and AI coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex, Gemini and OpenCode.

Source: https://agentmux.saxcave.cc/  |  App Store: https://apps.apple.com/app/id6766158521  |  Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=cc.saxcave.agentmux


---

# Guide — English

## Your AI should be working while you sleep

URL: https://agentmux.saxcave.cc/guide/en/why-remote-vibe-coding/
Language: en
Updated: 2026-11-04

What a CLI agent really costs you is not typing time — it's standby time. The CLI, tmux, and SSH plus Tailscale each undo one layer of that, taking standby from a single laptop down to the phone in your pocket.

A CLI agent's real cost is standby, not typing: thirty seconds of input, then hours you can't leave. Run it on a machine that stays on, keep the session alive with tmux, and reattach over SSH and Tailscale. The agent keeps working while you sleep; standby becomes a phone and fifteen seconds.

You have probably noticed it: the agent does the work, and you are the one tied down. What follows is what that tie is, why it comes apart, and what your day looks like afterwards.

## Where does the time actually go?

A round of work with a CLI agent almost always has the same rhythm:

```
You talk for 30 seconds → it runs for 5–20 minutes → it needs you to decide something → repeat
```

Lay a whole day out in those proportions and typing turns out not to be what eats the time. Those 30 seconds are the shortest part of the whole thing. Everything after is waiting — while it reads the project, while it edits a dozen files, while the tests run. Then it stops to ask whether it should handle this migration while it is here. You answer in one line. Another five minutes, another twenty.

By the end of the day you might have produced ten minutes of input and lost several hours. Those hours were not work. They were **standby**. You did nothing, and you could not leave, because at any moment it needed one sentence from you.

## The usual setup nails standby to one laptop

In the default arrangement that standby has a physical location. The agent runs in a terminal window on your laptop. The window is tied to the shell, the shell to that one machine staying awake. Two options follow:

**Sit and wait.** Stay in the chair, watching a screen where nothing happens, so that you can answer within thirty seconds when it asks. An hour of your time buys three replies.

**Or close the laptop.** The process suspends or dies, the session goes, and everything the agent had built up goes with it — which files it read, how far it got, why it chose this approach. Come back later and you open a new one, explain it all again, start from the top.

Both options pay the same bill. The work is not what ties you down. **The location of that machine** is.

## What three tools undo the tie?

The tie is not one solid thing. It is three layers, and each has a standard tool, decades old, that takes it apart. On their own all three are unremarkable. Stacked, they are the whole trick:

| Piece | The tie it undoes |
| --- | --- |
| CLI | The agent is a plain-text process with no need for a GUI → it can live on another machine |
| tmux | The session is pinned to the server and survives a dropped connection → standby doesn't need you present |
| SSH + Tailscale | Reattach securely from any network, with no public port and no static IP → standby isn't tied to a device or a place |

The order matters. The CLI comes first: only then can the agent leave your laptop for the Mac mini at home that never gets switched off. tmux next, so the session is pinned to that machine and keeps running when your connection drops. SSH and Tailscale last, so you can reattach to that same session from the train, the office, someone else's Wi-Fi — without opening one outward port on your router.

Drop any one and it falls apart. CLI without tmux: the agent dies on disconnect. tmux without a secure way in: you can only use it at home.

## The result: standby costs almost nothing

With all three layers gone, standby costs **a phone and fifteen seconds** instead of **a laptop and a fixed location**.

Fifteen seconds changes what the activity is. You stop setting aside time to babysit it. You glance at it in a queue, at a crossing, before bed, reply "use the second approach", and put the phone away. The agent keeps going. You get on with your day.

And once standby stops requiring you, the work moves into the hours you were never going to be there anyway. Hand it a refactor and go to dinner. Start a test-fixing session before bed, read the results over breakfast. That machine sat idle every night until now.

## What else reaches your agent when you're away?

There is more than one road to reaching your own agent remotely. Line them up against the same criteria and the differences show — particularly the last column, which is where people find out they are stuck, usually too late.

| Approach | Cost of standby | Does context survive | Network setup needed | Can it really edit your files |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Carry the laptop | You need a bag, a seat, and power | Stops when you close the lid | None, but the machine has to travel with you | Yes — the files are local |
| VNC remote desktop | Needs a screen big enough, and a mouse UI driven by finger | Survives as long as the desktop session does | Punch through for VNC, or stand up a VPN | Yes |
| Browser-based agent | Low — just open a browser | Lives on someone else's server | None | It edits a copy in a cloud sandbox, not the one on your machine |
| Cloud environments like Codespaces | Low, but you need a browser | The container gets reclaimed after enough idle time | None, but the project goes to the cloud and you're billed by usage | Yes, but it's the repo inside the cloud container |
| General SSH app | A phone is enough | Holds up, thanks to tmux | Securing the way in is on you | Yes, but the interface is a desktop terminal moved across as-is |
| Agentmux | A phone, fifteen seconds to reattach | tmux is on the server, regardless of the phone | Tailscale, with no public port | Yes — the copy on your own machine |

That last column is the watershed. An agent in someone else's cloud sandbox edits a copy, always. Your `.env` is not there. Neither is the internal package you installed this morning, or the database that only runs locally. Take the SSH and tmux road and the agent sits on your machine, in your environment, editing your files. The only thing that changed is that your phone is watching it.

Not sure where to start? Help me pick a track.

## Why not Cursor or VS Code

URL: https://agentmux.saxcave.cc/guide/en/why-not-gui-ide/
Language: en
Updated: 2026-11-04

An agent inside a GUI IDE is tied to a process that needs a screen. A CLI agent's interface is a byte stream you can reattach to. That's an architectural difference, not a matter of taste.

An agent inside Cursor or VS Code lives inside a GUI process, so it needs a screen, a logged-in desktop, and someone sitting in front of it. A CLI agent's interface is a stream of characters, which tmux can store whole and reattach on any device. That is an architectural difference, not a matter of taste.

You already have Cursor, or VS Code with an agent extension, and it works well. So why learn SSH and tmux to do the same job? The answer only shows up when you are away from your computer.

## The difference is architectural, not a preference

An agent inside a GUI IDE is part of that GUI program. It lives in the application's process, its state sits in that window's memory, its output is painted onto that canvas. So it needs a screen, a logged-in desktop session, and a person in front of it. Close the window and the agent ends. Nobody overlooked anything — it grew out of that process.

A CLI agent's interface is a byte stream. Characters in, characters out, nothing graphical anywhere along the way. And a character stream can be **attached to, detached from, and attached again**. tmux manages that because an 80×24 matrix of characters can be stored whole and redrawn onto any screen — your laptop, your phone, your friend's iPad. Changing device loses nothing. It was only ever characters.

So a CLI agent works remotely for one reason: **a canvas of pixels cannot be serialised and reattached, and a matrix of characters can**. Nothing to do with being geekier, or with text people being better. It is a difference in capability.

## What happens when you close the laptop mid-task?

Say you hand the agent a large refactor at the end of the day. Twenty minutes of work at least, and you are leaving now.

| Cursor left open | tmux + Claude Code |
| --- | --- |
| Close the laptop | Agent stops | Agent keeps running |
| Two hours later | Open it, context is gone, start again | Open your phone, it's finished |

The right-hand column has nothing to do with how clever the agent is. The session never lived on your laptop. It lives on the machine that was never switched off, and your laptop attached to it for a while. Closing the lid ended the connection, not the work.

Cursor has cloud background agents now, and those do keep running when you close the laptop. What they continue is a copy inside Cursor's own remote sandbox, not the one on your machine. That puts them with the browser agents and Codespaces discussed elsewhere on this site. It does not make them an exception to the left-hand column.

## "Couldn't you just use remote desktop?"

This is the most common objection, and in theory it is airtight. The desktop is still on that machine. VNC back into it, Cursor is still open, problem solved.

In practice the two ship different things. **VNC sends pixels. SSH sends characters.** A full screen update is hundreds of kilobytes to a few megabytes of image data; the same screen as characters is a few kilobytes of text. Three orders of magnitude.

You hit that gap daily. On the train, in a lift, anywhere you are down to one bar, VNC turns into a slideshow and a single scroll takes three seconds to redraw. SSH characters arrive instantly on the same connection.

Even with bandwidth to spare you are still facing a desktop UI built for a mouse and a 1440p display, crammed onto a six-inch touchscreen. Hitting a menu item means zoom, aim, tap. Driving an interface by touch that was never designed for touch is its own punishment.

## At your desk the IDE is often the better tool

GUI IDEs are not bad. At your desk an IDE is often the better tool — go-to-definition, refactoring, a debugger, none of which works on a phone. The division is simpler than it looks. **An IDE suits "you are here and you are driving". A CLI agent plus remote access suits "it is running and you are checking in".** The people who get the most out of either use both: the IDE on the Mac during the day, Agentmux to rejoin the same agent on the same project after they leave.

Agentmux isn't here to replace your IDE. It's here to replace **sitting in a chair, waiting**.

## Why the strongest coding agents live in the terminal

URL: https://agentmux.saxcave.cc/guide/en/what-is-cli/
Language: en
Updated: 2026-11-04

Why coding agents live in a terminal: full filesystem access and permission to execute. What a shell actually is, and when a GUI tool wins.

A CLI agent is a coding agent you talk to in text. It runs in a terminal on a machine you own — a Mac, a Linux box, a server — and inherits your permissions: read every file in the project, run any command, read the result back. Agents live in terminals because no other interface grants all three at once.

"CLI" still reads like a punishment: no mouse, no buttons, one blinking cursor. Yet Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI and OpenCode all live there. Not because their makers are purists: the terminal grants what no other interface does — **full filesystem access and permission to execute**. The same grant is why it asks before running anything.

## What is a terminal, once you strip the buttons away?

Two programs are stacked here, and beginners blame the wrong one. The **terminal** is the display: it draws a grid of characters and forwards your keystrokes. The **shell** behind it — zsh, bash, fish — waits for a line of text, runs it, and prints what that program wrote.

That thinness is why an agent can drive one end to end: every command it types is one you would have typed, every error it reads the one you would have seen.

## Three things you read off a terminal screen

Three things carry the meaning; the rest is noise.

```
yuki@mini ~/projects/auth (main)
$ npm test

 ✓ src/session/refresh.test.ts  (6 tests)
 ✗ src/session/expire.test.ts > drops a session after expiry

     Tests  1 failed | 41 passed (42)

$ echo $?
1
```

**The prompt** — that first line — says who, on which machine, in which directory, on which branch. It stops being decorative once the machine is not in front of you: after an SSH login it is how you tell your laptop from a server you forgot you opened.

**Standard output**, or *stdout*, is the text the program wrote. A second stream, *stderr*, keeps the complaints apart from the real output.

**The exit status.** Every command leaves one integer behind, handed over as `$?`. Zero means the program claims success. That is the line an agent reads — the `1`, not the words "1 failed": proof its loop is not closed.

## A capability boundary, not a question of looks

A browser agent cannot see a single file on your computer. It lives in a tab. An IDE plugin sees the files you have open, but it is usually confined to suggesting — no touching git, no running the tests, and certainly no installing packages.

A CLI agent holds the permissions you hold: it reads the whole repo, runs `git commit`, runs the suite, installs dependencies. Three tiers come with that, and the risk climbs:

- **Read.** Every file in your home directory, `.ssh` keys included.

- **Write.** Under git, a bad write is a `git checkout` away. Outside a tracked project, nothing rolls it back.

- **Execute.** Anything you could type, including a migration, a force-push, an `rm -rf` pointed at the wrong path.

No vendor designed this gap to please anyone: it is the permission set that comes with the terminal, and every other interface withholds part of it.

## Which commands can it run that a sandboxed agent cannot?

"Execution rights," in lines on a screen:

```
npm test
npx vitest run src/session/expire.test.ts

git status --short
git commit -m "fix: expire sessions on the dot"

npm install date-fns@3
npm run build

psql "$DATABASE_URL" -f db/schema.sql
curl -sf localhost:8000/health | jq .db
```

Where would those run inside a hosted sandbox? That `psql` connects to a database that exists only on your machine, using a URL from a `.env` file that was never uploaded. That `npm install` pulls an internal package from a private registry named in your `.npmrc`.

A sandboxed agent can write you a patch but cannot observe what the patch did — and an agent that cannot see the result of an edit cannot finish the task.

## The loop that closes without you pressing anything

You say "fix this bug." A dozen of those lines follow, hands off the keyboard:

- It greps for the failing message, reads three files, edits one.

- It runs `npm test`, reads the exit status, sees `1`.

- It narrows to one case, edits again, reruns the whole suite, gets `0`.

- It commits, applies the migration locally, curls the endpoint that was broken.

Nothing in that chain needed a click. In a browser tab or an IDE plugin it stalls at step two: it can produce the edit but cannot run the suite, so it waits for you to run it and report back. You have become the test runner — a permission problem, not a model-quality one.

## Why is a byte stream worth more than a window?

A terminal window is not where the program lives. The program is attached to a **pseudo-terminal** — a kernel object with two ends. Bytes go in one end and out the other; your window is whoever holds the far end right now. Three things follow.

- **It can be saved.** `npm test > build.log` writes that text to a file, which a program can read a year later. A GUI's canvas is a picture, not a record.

- **It can be chained.** `git ls-files | grep .env` feeds one program's output into another's input.

- **It can be moved.** Nothing says the two ends must be in the same place. tmux parks the session on the server; your screen attaches, detaches, and attaches again from another device.

That third one is the payload. **A byte stream can be redirected, stored, replayed, and reattached from somewhere else; a rendered window cannot.** Persistent sessions, SSH, the same agent on a phone: everything else in this guide follows from that property.

## What does full access cost you?

The permission that lets an agent migrate your database lets it delete one, which is why agents stop mid-task and ask: "Run this command?" That prompt is not timidity. An agent that ran everything without asking would be taking your `.ssh` directory and your production database on faith. It marks the line between tier two and tier three, drawn once the command is known.

Two habits cover most of it. **Read the command line, not the summary:** "I'll clean up the build cache" is a description, and only the line under it has consequences. **Approve once per category:** asked forty times a day to run tests, let `npm test` through on a rule once.

A prompt you were going to approve costs ten seconds. One allowed wrongly, against a live database, costs a day and a restore. That ratio is what AI Permission Review exists for: blacklist first, allowlist second, a model's judgement for the rest.

## When a GUI is genuinely the better tool

A terminal is not the right interface for everything you do to code. These are strictly worse in text:

- **A live debugger.** A breakpoint, one step through the loop, a variable inspected at frame four.

- **Anything visual.** Layout, spacing, a colour that is almost right. Describing a screenshot is a worse version of looking at one.

- **Reading a large diff.** Two thousand lines side by side — why you review an agent's work in a GUI even when the agent wrote it.

- **Still learning.** An editor underlining the exact token where you went wrong teaches faster than a stack trace.

The split is not skill against laziness. It is **"you are here and driving"** against **"it is running and you are checking in"**. At a desk an IDE is often the better instrument; the best users keep both. That division of labour is its own article.

The terminal gives an agent your machine, and its output is characters that can live anywhere — so the machine need not be the one you are sitting at. Getting there from elsewhere is SSH's job.

## An encrypted tunnel to another computer

URL: https://agentmux.saxcave.cc/guide/en/what-is-ssh/
Language: en
Updated: 2026-11-04

What SSH is, how host, user and port work, why keys beat passwords, and why you reach your own machine over a private address, not an open port.

SSH is an encrypted channel between your device and another computer. You send keystrokes, that machine runs the commands, its output comes back, and no hop in between can read any of it. To run a coding agent remotely, SSH is how your phone reaches the machine the agent is actually running on.

The last article made the case that an agent does its best work in a terminal, with full access to a filesystem and permission to execute. This one is about where that terminal lives. It does not have to be in your pocket: it can be the Mac mini at home that never gets switched off, or the workstation at the office, as long as you can reach it.

## Why "another machine" rather than a cloud service

Browser agents and cloud IDEs connect you to a machine too. The difference is whose machine it is.

SSH connects you to your own. Your files are there. Your API keys are there. Every package you installed, every environment variable you set. Nothing has to move onto someone else's server, and the changes stay where they were made — there is nothing to sync back afterwards.

The trade-off runs the other way too. A cloud environment is the better answer if you own no machine that stays on, or if a whole team needs one identical starting point. Your machine has to be awake, reachable, and set up by you.

## What you actually type: host, user, port

Every SSH connection needs three things, and the command writes them on one line:

```
ssh -p 22 sax@mac-mini
```

| Part | What it names |
| --- | --- |
| Host | Which machine — a name such as mac-mini, or an address such as 100.101.102.103 |
| User | Which account on it. You get its files, permissions, and shell, and nothing above |
| Port | Which door. SSH's default is 22, so the field usually goes empty |

Two of those three are where beginners get stuck. The host has to be an address your phone can route to — the next section. And the user has to exist on that machine: an agent runs as that user, touching exactly what that user can.

## Why not your LAN address or your public IP?

The first address you find is in your network settings: something like `192.168.1.23`. Try it from a laptop on the same Wi-Fi; that is what it is for. It is a private address handed out by your router, valid only inside your own network. A phone on mobile data has no route to it.

The second is the public address your home connection shows the internet, with a port forwarded through the router to that one machine. That road works, and it is the one to avoid. Scanning bots try logins against every address in the world, around the clock, and an exposed port starts collecting attempts within a day. One mistake in the router settings opens the whole network instead of one machine.

Use a third kind: a private address only your own devices can see. Tailscale gives each machine a MagicDNS name or a `100.x` address, and nothing else on the internet knows those exist. That goes in the host field, at home and away.

## Keys aren't the safer option — they're the easier one

SSH takes passwords or keys, and the choice gets framed as security versus convenience. It is not a trade-off. Keys win on both.

A key pair is two small text files. The private one stays on the device that connects. The public one is computed from it and copied onto the machine you want to reach, into `authorized_keys` inside that account's `~/.ssh` directory. The arithmetic runs one way: the public half comes from the private half, not back the other way. `ssh-keygen` makes a pair in seconds.

At login the two halves prove the match and you type nothing. A password has to survive repeated guessing; a key that long puts guessing out of reach. Set it up once and every connection afterwards works the same way.

Why put a passphrase on the private key? Because a key is a file. Copy it off an unlocked laptop and someone else holds your key. A passphrase makes the file worthless without it — and unlike a login password it never crosses the network. It unlocks the key locally; what travels is a signed answer to a challenge.

On a phone that gap widens. A typed password goes over the wire on every connection, handing anyone who can reach the port a fresh guess. A key answers a challenge instead, and the key never leaves the device. If the key is in place and still refused, the usual causes are few: wrong path, wrong user, wrong permissions.

## Where does the app keep my key?

Agentmux collects no personal data. Usage statistics are anonymous and optional; turning them off changes nothing about how it connects. Passwords, keys, and passphrases go into the operating system's hardware-backed credential storage. Your SSH traffic is never logged: the channel is encrypted between your device and your machine, and the app is not a relay.

## Why the fingerprint prompt appears the first time

The first time you reach a machine, before any password or key, the client prints a line about the host's authenticity, a short string of hex, and a yes or no. That string is the server's fingerprint: a readable summary of the host key the machine signs with. Nothing has gone wrong. SSH is authenticating the other direction.

A password or key proves you to the machine. A host key proves the machine to you. Without that second half, anyone between your phone and your Mac mini could answer in its place and read what you send. On a first connection there is no stored copy to compare against, so the client asks you to accept it and remembers it from then on.

It earns its keep later. Reconnect to a machine whose fingerprint has changed and the client refuses. Either you reinstalled the system, or something else is answering.

## You don't need to turn your computer into a server

People hear "SSH" and picture racks in a data centre. You are flipping a switch. On a Mac it is System Settings → General → Sharing → Remote Login. On Linux it is usually starting a service called `sshd`, which most distributions already ship.

Nothing else about the machine changes. It is still your everyday computer, with one more door you can knock on from outside. If you would rather not remember the order of operations, the setup page asks three questions and hands back a checklist.

## SSH is not a VPN or a remote desktop

Three things SSH does not do:

| Not this | What that would mean | What SSH does instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A VPN | Everything your phone sends routed into your home network | One channel to one port on one machine. Nothing else becomes reachable |
| A mounted filesystem | Your remote disk appears as a folder | Bytes on request. A file browser fetches and pushes each file itself |
| Screen sharing | Pictures of a desktop, steered with a finger | Text both ways: keystrokes out, printed output back |

That last row is a real limit, not a flaw in this tool. Software that exists only as a window you click cannot be driven over SSH — the same boundary the previous article stood on: an agent that speaks text is an agent that fits down the tunnel.

Then you put your phone away, the tunnel drops, and the agent dies with it — unless the session was never inside your connection to begin with. That is what tmux is for.

## Keep the agent running after you put your phone away

URL: https://agentmux.saxcave.cc/guide/en/what-is-tmux/
Language: en
Updated: 2026-11-04

What is tmux, and why your AI coding agent survives a dropped SSH: the session lives on the server, so your phone only ever attaches to it.

tmux is a terminal multiplexer: it keeps a terminal session running on the machine you connect to, rather than inside the connection you came through. For an AI coding agent, that is the difference between surviving and dying. SSH connections drop — a locked phone, a lost signal — and a dropped SSH normally kills the agent's shell.

You put your phone away, the SSH tunnel drops, and the agent dies with it. That is mechanics, not bad luck.

When the connection goes, the pseudo-terminal your login was using is closed. The kernel sends **SIGHUP** — hangup — to every process attached to it: your shell, and the agent inside it. Unless a process goes out of its way to handle that signal, the default is to terminate. Everything half-finished is thrown away. SSH was only the road the connection travelled on, and nobody meant it to hold the agent up.

## tmux lets the session live somewhere else

tmux opens a session on the server. Your agent runs inside that session, not inside the SSH connection that keeps dropping.

The mechanism is a process. The first time you type `tmux`, it starts a background program — the tmux *server* — that stays alive under your user account. Sessions belong to it, and each one gets its pseudo-terminal from that process, not from `sshd`.

So when the connection goes, `sshd` closes its own pseudo-terminal, and only your tmux client is attached to it. The client exits. The session does not notice.

## What is a session, a window, a pane?

Three nouns, used as one, and only the first keeps your agent alive.

| Word | What it is | What it means for an agent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| session | A named place to work on that machine, holding its own processes | The thing that survives. Name it once |
| window | A tab inside a session; most people give each agent one | Switch away and it keeps running |
| pane | A split inside a window: agent left, tests right | Two things visible on a phone screen |

A fourth word: a **client** is the terminal looking at a session. Zero clients is normal — a detached session, still running, nobody watching.

Names matter. `tmux new -s work` can be found again a week later; an unnamed session is just a number.

## Detach and attach are the same as turning off a television

Switch a TV off and the picture in your living room is gone. The broadcast never stopped. Turn it back on and you are on the same channel, wherever it has got to by now.

tmux calls those two actions **detach** and **attach** — close the window, open it again. Neither touches what is running on the machine.

The analogy hides one thing, in your favour. A television off learned nothing while off; a tmux session kept its output. Attach an hour later and you can read the hour you missed, scrollback and all.

## Which commands do I actually type?

Four to start with:

```
tmux new -s work          # make a session named work
claude                    # start the agent inside it
tmux ls                   # list sessions: work: 1 windows
tmux attach -t work       # look at it again, from anywhere
```

**Detach is a key press, not a command.** Press Ctrl-b, let go, then press d. That first key is the *prefix*: tmux takes it, and the next key says what to do. Two more are worth learning:

- `Ctrl-b d` — detach. The terminal becomes an ordinary shell again; the session runs on.

- `Ctrl-b c` makes a new window; `Ctrl-b %` splits a window into panes.

If the machine answers `tmux: command not found`, the fix is on the troubleshooting page.

## What this means for an agent

You lose signal on the train. Again in a lift. Again switching Wi-Fi. Attach to the same tmux session each time and you can drop ten times without the agent being interrupted once. It does not know you ever disconnected. It was never living inside your connection.

The three phone-side cases people worry about are one event three times over:

- **The phone locks.** The system suspends the app, the connection is torn down, nothing reaches the agent. It kept working.

- **No signal for twenty minutes.** The connection dies quietly, the tmux client with it, the session left detached and untouched.

- **The app is killed or swiped away.** A process on the phone is gone; the session was never inside it. Close a laptop's terminal window and tmux does the same.

Detach is not pause. While you are gone the agent keeps reading files, editing them, and spending your quota — which is the point, and the reason to answer a waiting prompt before you walk off.

## Can two devices watch the same session?

Yes, and it is not a party trick. Several clients can attach to one session at once. Start the job from the phone in a queue, attach from the laptop at work, and you are looking at the same screen mid-sentence — not a copy.

Keys from either device go to the same program, so one person types at a time. Attaching moves nothing: the session stays on the machine that made it, which is why phone and laptop agree. A session you started by hand in a laptop terminal is there for the app too.

## How the app handles these sessions

Agentmux is built on the same split. A disconnect on the phone's side is a detach, not a stop: reconnect and you are back at that session, further along. Type the commands above in its terminal and it is still the same session.

Two chores it takes off your hands. If the machine has no tmux, the app installs it, working out whether your machine uses apt, yum, dnf, pacman, apk, or brew. If an agent sits where the shell can't see it, the app probes that PATH problem. Persistent sessions are in the free single-server tier, so nothing here is paid. The setup page turns it into a checklist.

## What tmux does not do

tmux answers one question — will this process outlive my connection — and leaves the rest alone.

- **A reboot of the server ends every session.** They live in the tmux server's memory, so a power cut or an unattended upgrade ends the agent with them. What survives is what reached the disk: files changed, commits made, the branch you were left on. Git is the save file, not tmux.

- **It does not undo a command the agent already ran.** A command that ran has run. tmux kept the output; it does not roll back the files.

- **`tmux kill-session -t work` really does kill it.** So does quitting the last window, or the agent crashing. `tmux kill-server` takes every session with it. None of that asks first.

- **It does not keep the machine awake.** A Mac mini that stays on is a different case from a laptop that sleeps when the lid shuts — and a machine that powers off loses the session.

Two minutes proves the article. SSH in, run `tmux new -s work`, start an agent, press Ctrl-b then d, close the connection, and run `tmux attach -t work`: the same screen, further along, one question waiting.

So the agent survives you putting the phone away. One problem left: getting in from outside without opening a port to the whole internet. Tailscale answers that.

## Don't open a port to the public internet

URL: https://agentmux.saxcave.cc/guide/en/what-is-tailscale/
Language: en
Updated: 2026-11-04

How to reach your own computer from your phone without opening a port: a WireGuard mesh, a MagicDNS name or a 100.x address, and when to skip it.

Install Tailscale on your computer and on your phone, sign both in to the same account, then connect with SSH to the machine's MagicDNS name or its `100.x` address. Tailscale builds an encrypted WireGuard mesh between your own devices, so no port on your router is open to the internet and no public address is involved.

The agent survives a dropped connection, which only helps if there is somewhere safe to reconnect from. The obvious answer — expose port 22 to the internet — is the fastest way into trouble. Scanning bots knock on port 22 across every IP on earth, around the clock.

A second problem is duller and harder to dodge. Your home IP is dynamic, and the machine sits behind NAT, sharing one outward address with everything else at home. There was never a public address there to open.

## How painful the traditional fix is

The traditional fix meant the router itself: port forwarding so a public port reaches the machine, a DDNS service binding a hostname to today's IP or a static IP from your ISP, then firewall rules kept straight by hand.

Get one step wrong and you cannot get in, or you have exposed your whole home network. Get them all right and a door still faces the internet.

## Why port forwarding plus a dynamic IP keeps breaking

Four moving parts, each letting go at an inconvenient moment.

- **The address changes.** Your ISP reassigns it, and a DDNS client needs a few minutes to catch up. For a window after every change, nothing you saved points at home — and if that update fails while you are away, the hostname belongs to somebody else.

- **Sometimes the address was never yours.** Behind carrier-grade NAT your router holds an address inside the ISP's own network, so no forward can work.

- **One forward is one more door** into a network shared with a smart TV and an old camera.

- **It has to stay right forever.** A firmware update resets the rules; a new router means rebuilding them.

The real cost is the failure mode: debugging a home router from a phone on mobile data, when what you want is unreachable.

## What Tailscale does

Tailscale is a WireGuard mesh. Install it on each device, sign in to the same account, and the devices build an encrypted link straight between themselves. No public entry point, no port waiting to be scanned.

Each device makes a WireGuard key pair; the private half never leaves it. The public halves are exchanged, and those are the tunnels. The account is bookkeeping: it introduces devices, tracks where each is reachable, and hands out private addresses the public internet does not route to.

MagicDNS gives each device a name you can remember and resolves it for you. NAT, an address that changed overnight, home Wi-Fi then mobile data — all handled out of sight.

## Why the mesh works when your phone has no address either

Mobile data makes it worse. Your phone has no public address either: on 4G and 5G it sits behind carrier-grade NAT, sharing one outward address with many other subscribers. A door-knocking scheme fails at both ends.

A mesh works the other way round: both sides only have to send packets *outward*. The phone sends one, the machine sends one, each learns where the other appears to be, and the two attempt a direct path through their NATs. WireGuard supplies the encryption; the mesh supplies the introductions. Where no direct path exists, traffic falls back to a relay, still encrypted end to end.

## The mental model: one more address, reachable only by you

Your machine gains a private address. Only devices signed in to the same Tailscale account can see it or reach it. The scanning bots do not know it exists, because it never appeared on the public internet.

From here on, SSH goes to that address, not to a port 22 that gets knocked on all day.

## Which address do you actually type?

Not the LAN one. The machine holds three addresses at once, and only two are worth saving.

| Address | Where it works | Use it? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| LAN, e.g. 192.168.1.23 | That Wi-Fi only | No. On mobile data it routes nowhere useful |
| The ISP's address for the router | Nothing under carrier-grade NAT | No. It changes, and it is the router's |
| MagicDNS name, e.g. mac-mini.tail1234.ts.net | Any network, tunnel up at both ends | Yes. Save this one |
| 100.x.y.z | Same as the name | Yes, when name resolution is the broken part |

A LAN address describes a local network, not your machine. Save the name, and the entry survives the machine changing Wi-Fi, changing IP, or moving flats. `tailscale status` prints both.

When SSH fails although both devices look connected, check the address first. Tailscale says connected, SSH still can't reach it covers that, including a signed-out machine.

## What you give up by doing it this way

Three costs, better known before you are on a train.

**One more program on the machine.** It starts at boot, updates itself occasionally, and has its own bugs — one more thing to rule out before you blame SSH.

**A control plane you need at the wrong moment.** Traffic goes device to device; introductions do not. A new laptop, a replaced phone, stale credentials — none are on your network until they sign in. Fail that sign-in while you are out and the machine is fine but unreachable. Keep another way in.

**A phone that has to stay connected.** The tunnel is a VPN profile, and phones drop those: after a restart, when another VPN takes over, when you dismiss the prompt. Check it before debugging anything else. It carries only traffic to your own addresses.

## A private network is not a reason to go back to passwords

A machine nobody can reach from the internet still needs a lock on the door, for two reasons.

The mesh's security is now your account's security, and any device that signs in is inside — one device you already trusted. A laptop left in a taxi is inside the network you built, where every machine is reachable and nothing else asks questions. A key means it still has to prove something.

Then defence in depth. The mesh keeps strangers out; a key stops a stranger already in from going further. Two independent things have to fail before anyone reaches your project. A password is one guessable thing, and guessing is now easy. How keys do the proving covers the mechanics.

## When you don't need this at all

If the machine and the phone are on the same Wi-Fi and always will be, skip this. The LAN address works, nothing to install, nothing to sign in to — and you lose it the moment you walk outside.

A hosted server changes the arithmetic. Its address does not move, there is no router of yours to configure, and a failed experiment cannot lock you out. The risk moves to port 22 facing the internet permanently. Some still run the mesh there, to move SSH behind a private address; others stay public and lean entirely on keys. What is not workable: a password on an exposed port.

Or if you already reach it through a network someone else runs — a work VPN — take that path: two overlapping tunnels makes debugging worse, not the connection better. Not sure which case you are in? The setup page asks three questions and hands you a checklist.

The way in is settled. What is left is the thing in your hand, and what it assumes about why you are there.

## Why not Termius or Blink

URL: https://agentmux.saxcave.cc/guide/en/why-agentmux/
Language: en
Updated: 2026-11-04

Agentmux vs Termius and Blink: five capability differences, the cases where Termius is the better buy, and which tool fits which job.

A general SSH client assumes you opened it to type commands. Agentmux assumes you opened it to rejoin an agent already running. Buy Termius or Blink if you need Mosh, SOCKS5 forwarding, or host sync across platforms. Buy Agentmux if your day is spent inside coding agents on several servers. The trade-off is breadth of operations against depth of reattachment.

This is not a comparison of interfaces but of who thought harder about reattaching; every difference below follows from that. All five capabilities were checked against the current source.

## What each kind of tool is built around

A general SSH client is built around a host and a shell: hand you a working prompt, then stay out of the way. What happens after the prompt is yours.

Agentmux is built around an agent already running somewhere; its job is to shorten the distance from your pocket to that process. Three consequences follow. The last two are where a good general client stops being a substitute — not because it is badly made, but because those behaviours were never its product.

- **What you see first.** A host, or the sessions running on it.

- **What a dropped connection costs.** A prompt you re-navigate, or the screen you left.

- **What the app does while you are away.** Nothing, or a Lock Screen progress line and a sound at the end.

## Head to head, capability by capability

One row per capability. Where a competitor's behaviour cannot be checked from the outside, the cell says so.

| Capability | General SSH client | Agentmux |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Back to a tmux session | tmux ls, then tmux attach -t | Sessions listed on connect; one tap reattaches |
| After a drop | The prompt returns; finding the session is on you | A detach, not a death: you land on the screen you left |
| A twenty-minute agent run | No model of a run to report from | Dynamic Island and Lock Screen progress; a sound at the end |
| Prompt to allow a command | You are the reviewer, in the chair | AI Permission Review: blacklist, allowlist, AI judgement; suggests or presses the key (Pro) |
| One line in a file | Vim over SSH, on a phone keyboard | Runestone editor, Ink Markdown preview, branch tools, Files app (Pro) |
| Private keys | Not verifiable from outside | Keychain / Keystore, never the local database; iCloud sync carries server names only |
| Automation from outside | Nothing to call: no session or agent model exposed | 6 App Intents over four entity types: Server, Project, TMUXSession, RecentSession |
| Unreliable mobile networks | Mosh is a reason to buy this kind of app | Standard SSH plus tmux reattachment — not Mosh |
| Port forwarding | Local, remote, dynamic SOCKS5 | Local only |
| Host configuration at scale | Synced on iOS, Android, Windows, macOS, Linux; shared host lists | Multiple servers and batch actions (Pro); mobile only |

Read the last three rows first: they are where Agentmux loses.

## tmux-first reconnection

Connect to a server and Agentmux lists the tmux sessions already running on it. One tap reattaches. No `tmux ls`, no `tmux attach -t` to remember. Reconnect after a drop and you land on the same session, screen as you left it, without retyping anything.

An agent's value is the context it accumulated: which files it read, why it chose this approach. Reattach to that screen and the context survives; open a fresh prompt and you explain the task to a process that has forgotten it. What tmux does is the load-bearing part of this design.

## Background survival and Live Activity

Agents routinely run for tens of minutes. That waiting period is what this is built for. The Dynamic Island and Lock Screen show progress, and a sound can play when it finishes — so the app does not have to sit in the foreground while you stare at it.

An app built around a shell has nothing to report once closed: it holds no notion of a run. Here a named session on a named server is running, and the system reports on it. When it stops to ask whether to allow a command, AI Permission Review can look first: dangerous commands are held, safe ones get a suggestion or a key press (Pro).

## Runestone editor, Git tools, and Files app integration

Changing one line of code does not mean wrestling vim on a phone. The built-in Runestone editor opens the file and edits it. For a README an agent produced, Ink gives a two-column Markdown preview, source and rendered side by side. Git tools — switching branches, reading diffs — and Files app integration are Pro features, available during the 14-day trial.

The loop closes on one device: the agent changes files, you read the diff, you answer, it goes on. Every step that needs a second machine waits for a desk.

## Hardware-backed credential isolation

Private keys live in native secure storage (the iOS Keychain / Android Keystore) and are never written to the local database. On iOS, if you turn on iCloud sync, CloudKit carries non-sensitive metadata such as server names. The keys stay put.

Ask any tool the same question: which private keys leave this device if sync is on? A feature list will not answer it.

## Siri and Shortcuts automation

`GetCurrentSessionContextIntent` lets you tell Siri "get the current terminal contents from Agentmux". Whatever is on the terminal lands in iOS Shortcuts, ready for Notes, Messages, or anything you build. `ContinueLastSessionIntent` is blunter: "continue working in Agentmux" reattaches to your last session.

General SSH apps cannot do this, structurally. They have no semantic model of sessions, projects, and agents to expose to the system; Agentmux implements 6 App Intents across four entity types — Server, Project, TMUXSession, RecentSession.

## Fixes you'll feel if you read CJK

Version 1.3.10 fixed three things an English-only user never notices and a Chinese, Japanese, or Korean reader spots at once. Selection alignment drifting on full-width characters. A link that wraps across lines breaking into several pieces when copied. A single slash inside CJK text read as a file path. You only fall into those once you have handled CJK text.

## Which tool for which job

**Mostly manual terminal work on one host.** You log in to run commands you chose: restart a service, tail a log, check a disk. Take a general SSH client. The free single-server tier covers one server, persistent sessions, and the core terminal, if you want to test the idea first.

**Living inside agents on several servers.** One refactoring on the Mac mini, another running tests on a Linux box, a third started from a train. That is Agentmux, and specifically Pro: multiple servers, custom agents, remote editing, file history, branch tools, batch actions.

**An agent in a browser tab or a cloud sandbox.** The convenience is real, and the cost is that the files and the credentials no longer sit on your machine. Agentmux never hosts the work: it is a client, and the code and the agent stay on hardware you own — a Mac, a Linux box, a server. Renting one is defensible if you are at peace with your project and its keys living there.

Tailscale is the recommended way in: no port open to the public internet, machines addressed by MagicDNS names or 100.x addresses rather than LAN IPs.

## When Termius is the better buy

If one of these is your main job, buy the general tool.

- You work on very unreliable mobile networks and need **Mosh** to hold the connection. Agentmux only speaks standard SSH and compensates with automatic tmux reattachment, which is not the same thing as Mosh.

- You need **remote or dynamic (SOCKS5) port forwarding**. Agentmux only does local — a hard gap, not a preference.

- You want to sync a large host configuration across iOS, Android, Windows, macOS, and Linux, or share a host list with a team. Agentmux is a mobile client: multiple servers and batch actions on Pro, nothing shared.

- You're an SRE or sysadmin running operations across dozens or hundreds of servers. An inventory you script against beats a list you tap through.

Agentmux is built for one workflow: **rejoining a running coding agent from your phone.** It is not a general-purpose operations tool, and a week of manual SSH will not earn that back.

Decided on Agentmux? The next problem is the machine at the other end: the setup wizard asks three questions and hands back a checklist, and most of what goes wrong afterwards is already in troubleshooting.

## 15 minutes to an agent that works all night

URL: https://agentmux.saxcave.cc/guide/en/setup/
Language: en
Updated: 2026-11-04

Answer three questions and get a checklist built for your setup: your machine, the agent you want to run, and where you plan to connect from.

Setting up an agent that works all night takes about fifteen minutes: SSH into a machine you own, tmux so a dropped phone connection detaches instead of stopping the agent, and Tailscale so no port is open to the public internet. Answer three questions and the checklist is built for your machine, your agent, and where you connect from.

Every step tells you **why you're doing it**, **what the command is**, **how to confirm it worked**, and **where to look if it didn't**. (Is that machine running Windows? Read this first.)

The setup wizard needs JavaScript. You can also go straight to the troubleshooting page.

## Native Windows has no tmux — use WSL2

You picked Windows, so the wizard did not hand you a checklist. Not because one is missing. This path is a different shape from the other three, and half a checklist would do you more harm than none.

It works, but it goes through WSL2 and takes a few more steps than a Mac or a Linux box. If all you want is an agent working through the night, rent the cheapest cloud VPS you can find and take the VPS path above. That is usually faster than getting Windows there, and it is not a brush-off — it saves most people an evening.

### Why native Windows won't do

This guide rests on three pieces: the CLI, tmux, SSH. SSH is fine. Windows 10 and 11 both ship an OpenSSH Server you can switch on, and you will get a PowerShell prompt.

tmux is the problem. **There is no native Windows build**, and tmux is the load-bearing piece of this whole guide. Without it your connection drops, the agent gets SIGHUP, and it dies (the mechanism). "Put your phone away and it keeps running" stops being true. You would have a Windows machine you can SSH into, which is not what this guide is offering.

Whether the agents themselves run on Windows varies by tool and changes quickly, so there is deliberately no list here. Check the documentation for the one you plan to use. Note the order of the argument though: **an agent running perfectly on native Windows does not touch the tmux problem.** Running and surviving a disconnect are separate questions.

### The recommended route: WSL2

Inside WSL2 you have a complete Linux. tmux, sshd, and the agents behave the way they do on real Linux. Install a distribution and every step of the "Linux box" path applies — go back up and answer the first question that way.

### Three snags that don't exist on Mac or Linux

None is a dead end. Knowing them in advance saves you assuming you broke something:

- **Networking.** WSL2 runs in a virtual machine with its own IP, behind NAT. The sshd inside it is not reachable from outside that Windows host by default. Two ways around it. Set up `netsh interface portproxy` on the Windows side to forward the port in — though WSL's IP can change on every restart, so you will be redoing it. Or turn on mirrored networking with `networkingMode=mirrored` in `.wslconfig`, which lets WSL share the host's interfaces and drops the port-forwarding step entirely. The second is much cleaner and needs a reasonably recent Windows 11.

- **WSL doesn't stay running on its own.** When the last process exits, the distribution shuts down within seconds and takes the virtual machine with it. This guide wants a machine that is *always on*, so WSL has to start at boot and stay up with nobody logged in — usually a scheduled task or a keepalive. On a Mac or a Linux box there is nothing here to think about. This one is WSL's alone.

- **systemd is opt-in.** Older WSL has no systemd at all; `systemctl` does not exist. The systemd commands in the wizard's "enable the SSH service on the Linux box" step fail outright. Newer versions turn it on with `systemd=true` in `/etc/wsl.conf`, but it is off by default and older installations will not have it.

### One more option: keep Windows as the client

The Windows discussed here is always *the machine you connect to*. If your Windows PC is the computer you work at, and the agent runs somewhere else — a Mac mini at home, a Linux box at the office, a VPS — none of the above applies. The guide works for you as written. The machine you need to set up was never the one in front of you.

## Run Claude Code on your iPhone or iPad

URL: https://agentmux.saxcave.cc/guide/en/claude-code-on-iphone/
Language: en
Updated: 2026-11-04

Run Claude Code from an iPhone or iPad. It runs on your own machine; the phone carries the terminal — Remote Login, Tailscale, tmux, and the PATH gotcha.

Yes. Claude Code is a program that runs on a machine you own, never on the phone. Turn on Remote Login, reach that machine through Tailscale instead of an open port, start a tmux session with a name, and run `claude` inside it. Your iPhone carries a terminal; the agent keeps working after you lock the screen.

The phrase sounds obvious and is not: "Claude Code on my phone" describes two machines doing different jobs. Separate them and what is left gets short — what survives a dropped connection, why the command is missing over SSH, whether an agent should answer its own permission prompts from a train.

## Your phone carries a terminal. That is all.

Claude Code is a program on the disk of some machine you own. A shell starts it. It reads your project through that filesystem, runs `git` and the tests, and writes its edits back into the same directory. The misconception: that some part of it now lives in your pocket.

From the phone, two things cross the wire: keys go out, characters come back. Nothing of the agent is installed there, and no copy of your repository travels. The phone draws a picture of a session living on another computer.

- **On the phone.** Keystrokes, display, your thumb. Lock the screen or swipe the app away and the display stops; that is the whole list.

- **On the machine.** The process, the files being edited, the tests, everything already read and decided. None of it notices your screen going dark.

Two consequences. The machine has to stay on and reachable — a laptop in a drawer with the lid shut runs nothing. The phone is the cheap half to replace.

## Three things in place, in order

Skip one and the arrangement fails. Do them in this sequence.

- **A door into the machine.** On a Mac: System Settings → General → Sharing → **Remote Login**. On Linux, the SSH service, a daemon called `sshd`.

- **A private network, not an open port.** Install Tailscale on the machine and the phone, sign both into one account, then connect to the MagicDNS name or the `100.x` address — never a LAN address like `192.168.1.23`, which means nothing on mobile data. Forwarding port 22 instead hands your machine to every scanning bot that finds it.

- **A tmux session with a name, and the agent inside it.**

```
tmux new -s work     # name it
claude               # inside it
```

From the phone, on another network:

```
tmux ls              # what exists
tmux attach -t work  # open a window onto it
```

The name matters: `tmux attach` alone takes the most recent session. If tmux is missing, Agentmux installs it.

## Why a plain SSH window kills the agent

Skip tmux: you SSH in, run `claude`, then pocket the phone and lock the screen.

The connection times out and closes. sshd closes the pseudo-terminal it was attached to, and the kernel sends **SIGHUP** to every process still on it — your shell, and Claude Code inside it. The default response is to terminate: the agent dies mid-edit, twenty minutes of reading gone.

Keeping the app open fixes nothing: Wi-Fi switches networks, cellular loses signal, one Ctrl-C lands wrong. tmux moves the session onto the machine, so what disappears is the window, not the process (the mechanism). The rule: **the agent goes inside the session before the work starts — a running process cannot be moved into tmux afterwards.**

## What working from a phone is actually like

What fits a phone is one decision at a time — which is what an agent cycle is made of. It proposes a plan; you take it or send it back in a sentence. A two-line correction — "leave the serializer alone, the export job uses it" — and the phone goes away.

The on-screen keyboard is the first real cost. Backticks, pipes, quotes, backslashes and the tilde all sit two layers deep, so `~/src/auth/session.ts` takes longer than it should and one wrong segment costs a round trip. Long prompts are harder to proofread than they look, so many people draft them in a notes app.

A diff is where a phone runs out of room: forty changed lines across two files is three screens of scrolling on six inches, and a wrapped line hides whether a change sits at the end of a line or in the middle. Turn an iPad sideways and it fits without wrapping.

One habit pays for itself: a second session for the noisy parts, so a test run cannot bury the agent's prompts.

```
tmux new -s tests -d    # -d starts it detached
tmux attach -t tests    # watch it, then detach
```

## The agent stops and asks. From the phone, you answer.

Claude Code does not run everything it thinks of. Before it runs a command — and, depending on configuration, before it edits a file — it stops and asks: here is the command, go ahead? That stop is where the job waits, and when only you can answer it, the waiting becomes the bottleneck.

AI Permission Review answers those prompts and nothing else: it reads the prompt, then suggests or presses the key. A **blacklist** blocks dangerous commands and always hands a match to you. An **allowlist** passes commands you already trust, decided on the device. Anything matching neither goes to an **AI judgement**: allow, deny, or unsure, and the last two come back to you. The session's mode then decides whether it only **suggests** the key or **presses** it.

Distance does not transfer the responsibility. A command approved on cellular runs on a machine holding your `.env`, your keys, and a repository you do not own alone — and the judgement sees the screen, not the reasoning that got the agent there. Start in the mode that only suggests, allowlist the commands you approve daily, and read the screen before pressing anything when signal and attention are poor. The blacklist exists because "approve everything" is a bad default: an `rm -rf` aimed at a home directory is no gentler because you said yes on a platform.

## claude: command not found, but it runs in Terminal

Same machine, same account, different answers: `claude` starts in Terminal and prints `claude: command not found` over SSH. It reads as the remote setup being broken, and it is the most common failure on the way in.

The cause, in two sentences. An install through npm, or under a node version nvm pins, puts its directory on the PATH from a startup file that only an *interactive login* shell reads. A connection running one command, like `ssh host claude`, starts a non-interactive shell that never reads that file.

The fix that always works is to stop relying on the PATH. In the Terminal where it runs:

```
which claude
# /Users/you/.nvm/versions/node/v20.11.0/bin/claude
```

Use that absolute path, as the agent command or typed into the session. It breaks when nvm changes the node version; the durable fix, which depends on your shell and your distribution, is on the troubleshooting page.

## Overnight works. A reboot does not.

A session on a machine that stays awake runs all night — hand it a refactor at eleven, read the result with coffee. Three limits.

**The machine has to stay awake.** A Mac that idles into sleep takes its network interface with it, and Remote Login makes no difference: nothing is left to answer. System Settings → Battery on a laptop, Energy Saver on a desktop: lengthen or switch off idle sleep, and turn on "Wake for network access" if offered.

**A reboot takes the session with it.** tmux does not restore sessions after a restart, and updates restart without asking. Commit before you stop for the night, so the worst case costs an hour.

**Waiting is not crashing.** Attach and look. A fresh shell prompt means the process exited: finished, or died, and the lines above say which. A prompt asking a question has waited one word from you for six hours at no cost. From a lock screen both look the same; only one needs you to act.

## What belongs on the phone, what belongs at the desk

| From the phone | At the desk |
| --- | --- |
| Answer a permission prompt, having read it | Review a diff you did not expect to see |
| Choose between the two approaches it offered | Judge a change spanning several files |
| Read one short diff, commit, push | Read a long diff, or a file you have never opened |
| Watch a test run in a second session | Debug the failure those tests printed |
| Hand it the next task before bed | Write a prompt that has to be exact |
| Reattach after ten dropped connections | Fix the connection, or the PATH problem behind it |

A machine that stays awake, a session with a name, a private way in. Missing one, the setup wizard asks three questions about your machine and hands back a checklist.

## AI Permission Review: who answers when your agent asks

URL: https://agentmux.saxcave.cc/guide/en/permission-review/
Language: en
Updated: 2026-11-04

When an agent stops to ask "Run this?", AI Permission Review blocks dangerous commands with a blacklist, lets through the ones you trust with an allowlist, sends the rest to AI, and then suggests or presses the key depending on your mode. Every step, from trigger to decision.

AI Permission Review is how Agentmux answers the permission prompt an agent raises on a screen you are not looking at. Each request is checked against a blacklist that blocks dangerous commands, an allowlist of commands you already trust, and then an AI judgement. Depending on the session's mode, it suggests the key or presses it for you.

Halfway through a task, the agent stops to ask "Run this command?" — and you happen to be away from the screen. The whole job sits there waiting for you. That is the moment it is built for.

It does exactly one thing: answer the agent's permission prompts, one key at a time. It never types commands for you and never touches anything beyond what's on screen.

- **The agent stops and waits**Agentmux detects a permission prompt

- **Read the screen**Find the current prompt and redact sensitive text

- **Blacklist**A dangerous command matched*Handed to you*

- **Allowlist**A command you trust matched; pick the key locally

- **AI judgment**Allow, deny, or unsure*Deny or unsure: handed to you*

- **Re-check before sending**If the screen changed, nothing is sent*Handed to you*

- **Suggest, or press for you**Depends on the mode you picked

## It starts only when an agent stops and waits

It only starts when an agent stops and waits for you. Agentmux already tracks the state of agents like Claude Code and Codex. When a prompt such as "Allow this?" or "Pick 1 or 2" appears, the session is marked as waiting, and the review begins at that moment.

These also need to be true:

- The AI Permission Review switch in Settings is on.

- The session's mode is Advisor or Auto Reply, not Off.

- You have Pro, or you're still in the free trial.

Each prompt is judged once; it doesn't re-ask every few seconds. As soon as you press a key or type in the terminal yourself, any judgment in progress is cancelled and your input wins.

Sessions that aren't on screen are reviewed too. When you switch to another tab, it keeps watching in the background.

## It reads the current prompt, not the scrollback

It first picks out the current prompt on screen: the command to run, the question itself, and the choices you can pick. Older content that has scrolled up doesn't count.

Before anything goes to the AI, text that looks like a password, API key, or token is redacted. If redaction fails, the original text is not sent, and no key is pressed this time.

## The blacklist runs first, on your phone

The blacklist is matched right on your phone and always runs first. A match is never sent to the AI; it's handed straight to you. The built-in rules cover the most dangerous kinds of operations:

- `rm -rf` on `/`, `~`, or your home directory

- `sudo`

- `git push --force` (`--force-with-lease` doesn't count)

- `DROP TABLE`, `DROP DATABASE`, `TRUNCATE TABLE`

- Piping something downloaded straight into a shell, like `curl … | sh`

- Commands that write directly to a disk, like `mkfs` and `dd if=`

You can edit or remove these built-in rules, and add your own.

## The allowlist decides without the AI

Some commands you approve every day, like running tests or a build. Add them to the allowlist, and the next match is decided right on your phone — which key to press, with no wait for the AI and no API usage.

In Auto Reply mode, you can also turn on "Allow all commands in this session" for a single session. It skips AI judgment, but the blacklist still applies, and it turns off when the session ends.

If the allowlist matches but there's no clear, safe key to press on screen, the prompt is handed to you.

## What does the AI actually decide?

Only prompts that match neither list go to the AI. It sees the redacted screen and your **Main Intent** — what you want the agent to do this time, such as "fix the login page tests".

You can choose between two engines:

- **JEV decision engine** (through OpenRouter or TypeSafe): built for terminal prompts, and fast. It judges in three levels: read-only, safe operations are allowed; commands that match your Main Intent are allowed; everything else — unrelated, unclear, or high-risk — is handed to you. Anything that looks suspicious or like a malicious injection is denied outright.

- **An OpenAI-compatible LLM**: OpenAI, OpenRouter, or a model you run on your own machine.

The AI reaches one of three conclusions: allow, deny, or unsure. Only "allow" goes further, and the AI has to name exactly which option on screen to pick. It never picks a permanent choice such as "Always allow" or "Don't ask again".

## Advisor suggests, Auto Reply presses the key

Each session has its own mode:

- **Advisor** (default): suggestions only. A notice at the top of the screen tells you what it recommends, with an Accept button next to it. Nothing is sent until you tap it.

- **Auto Reply**: when the verdict is allow, it presses the key for you and shows a notice saying what it pressed.

Either way, it looks at the screen again right before sending a key. If the prompt changed, the options moved, or the cursor isn't on the target, nothing is sent. This keeps a change in the few seconds of judgment from turning into the wrong choice.

After Auto Reply sends a key, it waits 3 seconds before it can send another in the same session.

## When does it hand the prompt back to you?

- A blacklist rule matched.

- The AI said deny, or wasn't sure.

- It can't tell which key the prompt wants.

- The choice is a permanent grant like "Always allow".

- The screen changed before the key was sent.

- Redacting sensitive text failed.

When that happens, Agentmux alerts you the usual way, exactly as it would with the review turned off.

## How do I turn it on?

Before you start, have one of these ready:

- An API key for the JEV engine, from OpenRouter or TypeSafe.

- Your own OpenAI-compatible LLM endpoint, such as the OpenAI API or a model running on your own computer.

- Open Settings → AI Permission Review and turn on the switch. The first time, you'll see an explanation of what data is shared. Tap to agree, and you're taken straight to Advanced Settings.

- In Advanced Settings, choose an engine, enter your API key, and tap "Test AI Endpoint Connection" to make sure it works.

- Back in Settings, pick a default under Permission Review Mode (Advisor is a good start), then write down your Main Intent.

- Connect to a server and start an agent. New tabs start in the default mode. To change the mode or Main Intent for one session, tap the Permission Review button in the terminal toolbar. There you can also turn on "Use My Latest Prompt" so the Main Intent follows each prompt you send in that tab.

Try Advisor for a few days first to see whether its suggestions match how you work, before turning on Auto Reply for specific sessions.

## What data leaves your device?

Only redacted screen excerpts and your Main Intent are sent, to the AI service you set up, using your own API key. If "Use My Latest Prompt" is on, the prompts you send in that tab become the Main Intent and are sent too. Agentmux doesn't provide or relay any AI service. A record of each decision stays on your device only; you can review or clear it in the audit log. Model reasoning is never stored.

## Stuck? Start here

URL: https://agentmux.saxcave.cc/guide/en/troubleshooting/
Language: en
Updated: 2026-11-04

Can't connect, key rejected, tmux not found, agent command missing — the eight things that most often go wrong when setting up remote development, and how to fix each one.

Remote development over SSH, tmux and Tailscale fails in eight recognizable ways: `Operation timed out`, `Permission denied (publickey)`, a password that is correct but rejected, `tmux not found`, `claude: command not found`, Tailscale showing connected but unreachable, Remote Login on but the Mac refusing, and `sudo: a terminal is required`. Each one has a symptom, a cause, and a fix.

Follow the previous articles and it works first time eight or nine times out of ten. When it does not, it is almost always one of these eight. Find your error message and jump to it. Nobody needs to read this page from the top.

## Connection timed out (Operation timed out)

### Symptom

You run `ssh user@host` and the screen just sits there. After a long wait you get `Operation timed out` or `Connection timed out`, never having been offered a password prompt.

### Causes

- A typo in the hostname, say `my-serverr`. SSH reports `Could not resolve hostname` for that straight away rather than hanging, so if you see that message go check the spelling — it is not what this section covers. What actually hangs is a wrong IP: a missing octet, one wrong digit, an address where nothing is listening.

- SSH isn't on the standard port 22 on the other end and you left out `-p`.

- The target machine is asleep, or simply switched off.

- A firewall in between — home router, corporate network, hotel Wi-Fi — is dropping the connection, so the machine never receives your request.

### Fix

Don't guess — confirm one hop at a time. First check whether the machine responds at all:

```
ping host-address
```

Nothing back from `ping`? Check the IP for typos, and check whether the machine is asleep or powered off. Some machines block `ping` on purpose, so a failure here does not prove the machine is unreachable — go straight to the next step.

Next, check whether anything is actually listening on the SSH port:

```
nc -vzw 5 host-address 22
```

Replace `22` with the port the other end really uses. The `-w 5` caps the wait at five seconds, so a blocked port cannot leave the command hanging with nothing to show you.

Three outcomes. `succeeded` or `open`: the port is reachable, the problem is elsewhere. `Connection refused`: the machine received you, but nothing is listening there. Another timeout: something in between is dropping the packets, usually a firewall — look at the router configuration or the network you are on, not the server.

## Permission denied (publickey)

### Symptom

The connection is refused the instant you make it, printing `Permission denied (publickey).` without ever offering you a password prompt.

### Cause

The server will not accept the key you are presenting. Most often the public key was never put on the server at all.

The other cause is easy to miss: permissions on `~/.ssh` or `authorized_keys` that are too loose. SSH is strict here. Wrong permissions and it ignores the file completely, however correct the key inside is.

### Fix

If you've never copied the public key across, the quickest route is `ssh-copy-id`: it logs in once with a password and appends your local public key to the server's `authorized_keys`.

```
ssh-copy-id user@host
```

That assumes password login is still enabled on the server. If it has already been turned off (see Password is correct but rejected below), you'll need someone with console access to that machine to paste the public key into `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` directly.

If the key really is in there — one per line, complete, not truncated — and you are still refused, permissions are the likely culprit. Check them against the table. The last row is the one people miss: get `~/.ssh` and `authorized_keys` both right, leave your home directory group- or world-writable, and `StrictModes` still refuses.

| Path | Required permissions | Command |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ~/.ssh | 700 | chmod 700 ~/.ssh |
| ~/.ssh/authorized_keys | 600 | chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys |
| ~ (the home directory itself) | Not writable by group or others | chmod go-w ~ |

Try connecting again once the permissions are fixed. If it still fails, add `-v` locally to watch the exchange and confirm SSH is really offering the key you think it is:

```
ssh -v user@host
```

That runs to fifty or sixty lines. You only need two of them. `Offering public key: ...` means your key really was sent, so nothing is wrong at your end. If `Authentications that can continue: publickey` follows it, the server received the key and declined it — wrong place or wrong permissions, so carry on with the steps above.

## Password is correct but rejected

### Symptom

You're certain the password is right — you may even have pasted it — but SSH keeps returning `Permission denied, please try again.`, or ends without ever prompting you for one.

### Cause

This usually has nothing to do with the password. The server's SSH configuration has password authentication switched off (`PasswordAuthentication no`), a common hardening choice that forces everyone onto keys and takes brute-force guessing off the table. With that set, a correct password gets refused a hundred times out of a hundred.

There is a trap here that costs more time than anything else on this page. Newer systems — Ubuntu after 22.10, Debian 12, nearly every cloud provider's default image — put a line near the top of `sshd_config` reading `Include /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf`, which pulls in every config file in that directory. And sshd keeps the *first* value it reads for a setting. Later ones do not override it.

So if `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/` holds something like `50-cloud-init.conf` that also says `PasswordAuthentication no`, it wins over the line you just edited in the main file. You save, you restart, you are still refused.

### Fix

The preferred fix is to switch to key authentication — see Permission denied (publickey) above for getting your public key into the server's `authorized_keys`.

Only change the configuration if you administer this server and have decided you do want password login. First find out whether another file will override the value you're about to edit:

```
sudo grep -r PasswordAuthentication /etc/ssh/sshd_config /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/
```

If a file under `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/` also sets `PasswordAuthentication`, change that value too (or comment the line out). Once that's clean, edit `/etc/ssh/sshd_config` and set `PasswordAuthentication` to `yes`.

**Don't close your current connection yet.** A broken sshd configuration can lock you out of the machine for good. Keep this window as your way back in until the new one is confirmed working. Check the syntax before anything else:

```
sudo sshd -t
```

Only once that prints no errors should you restart the service to apply it:

```
sudo systemctl restart ssh
```

On some distributions the service is called `sshd` rather than `ssh`. If the line above cannot find it, try `sudo systemctl restart sshd`. Then open a brand-new connection — not the one you kept as a fallback — and confirm password login works. Only then close the old window.

This whole setup runs on Tailscale, so there is a safer option than opening password login to the entire internet: allow passwords from the Tailscale range only, and require keys everywhere else. Add this at the end of `sshd_config`:

```
Match Address 100.64.0.0/10
    PasswordAuthentication yes

Match All
    PasswordAuthentication no
```

## tmux not found

### Symptom

Agentmux reports that it can't find tmux, or you connect yourself, type `tmux`, and get `command not found: tmux`.

### Cause

tmux is not installed on the target machine yet, and that is not yours to handle. Agentmux installs it: it detects whether the machine uses apt, yum, dnf, pacman, apk (Alpine), or brew, then runs the matching command over SSH. Usually you wait for it to finish.

When that fails, the usual reason is `sudo`. The install command includes it, the channel is non-interactive, and `sudo` has no terminal to ask for a password on (see sudo: a terminal is required to read the password below). Second most common: Homebrew on a Mac while connected as root. Homebrew refuses to run as root by design.

A rarer case is easy to misread. tmux *is* installed, just somewhere Agentmux did not see when it probed the PATH — Linuxbrew under `~/.linuxbrew`, MacPorts under `/opt/local/bin`. The message reads the same, but the problem is the PATH, not a missing install. Handle it as described in claude: command not found, but it runs fine in the desktop terminal below.

### Fix

Start with the error Agentmux showed you. If it asks for a sudo password, or mentions passwordless sudo, type the password in and retry — that is usually faster than opening a separate window. If that fails too, or the message mentions a terminal or TTY, work through sudo: a terminal is required to read the password yourself. Once that is sorted the automatic install normally succeeds and you can stop there.

Install by hand only if it still won't install after the `sudo` problem is ruled out:

```
# Debian / Ubuntu
sudo apt install -y tmux

# RHEL / CentOS
```
